title: Alcohol and Eczema: Why Drinking Can Trigger a Flare
excerpt: Does alcohol make eczema worse? Why drinking can trigger itching and flares, which drinks are most likely to cause trouble, medication cautions, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does alcohol make eczema worse? Why drinking can trigger itchy flares, which drinks cause the most trouble, medication cautions, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol doesn't cause eczema, but for a lot of people it can make an existing flare worse. Many people with eczema (atopic dermatitis) notice more itching, redness, or a flare in the day or two after drinking. The likely reasons are fairly well understood: alcohol widens blood vessels in the skin, it can raise histamine levels, it disrupts sleep, and some drinks carry extra triggers like sulfites. None of this means you have to stop drinking. It means it's worth learning your own pattern, choosing drinks more carefully, and protecting your skin barrier on nights you do drink.

**The quick rules:** If drinking seems to set off your eczema, cut back first on the drinks most likely to cause trouble (red wine, beer, and cheap sparkling wine are common culprits), keep drinks spaced out, drink water alongside, moisturize before bed, and don't stack alcohol with a sedating antihistamine. If you take a prescription eczema medicine such as methotrexate or cyclosporine, ask your doctor how much alcohol, if any, is safe for you.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **See a doctor or dermatologist soon if** your eczema is spreading or not responding to your usual treatment, you're losing sleep to itching most nights, or you think a specific drink causes hives, swelling, or wheezing. **Get same-day care if** eczema patches become painful, weep yellow fluid, crust over, or develop clusters of small punched-out blisters or sores, especially with a fever. That can be an infection, including eczema herpeticum, a herpes infection of eczema skin that needs prompt treatment. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** for swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, or feeling faint after a drink.

## Does Alcohol Make Eczema Worse?

For many people, yes. Eczema is a condition where the skin barrier doesn't hold moisture well and the immune system in the skin overreacts, which leads to dry, itchy, inflamed patches. Flares tend to come from a stack of triggers rather than one cause: dry air, sweat, stress, poor sleep, certain fabrics or soaps, allergens, and sometimes food or drink.

Alcohol fits into that stack. It's rarely the only reason for a flare, but it can push skin that's already on edge over the line. Dermatology patient surveys and clinical experience consistently list alcohol among the things people with eczema report as triggers, alongside stress and weather. At the same time, plenty of people with eczema drink moderately and notice no difference at all.

That split is important. Large population studies haven't found a clear, consistent link between how much people drink and whether they have eczema in the first place. The connection seems to be about **flares in people who already have eczema**, and it varies a lot from person to person. The useful question isn't "does alcohol cause eczema?" It's "does alcohol set off *my* eczema, and which drinks?"

## Can Alcohol Cause Eczema?

There's no good evidence that drinking causes eczema to develop in someone who never had it. Eczema is driven mainly by genetics (including changes in skin barrier proteins such as filaggrin), the immune system, and the environment, and it usually starts in childhood.

What alcohol *can* do is produce skin reactions that look a bit like eczema or get mistaken for it:

- **Flushing.** Red, warm skin on the face, neck, and chest after drinking. This is common and usually fades within hours. In people of East Asian descent it's often caused by a slow version of the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. Our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains this in detail, and our guide to [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) covers the other common causes.
- **Hives.** Raised, itchy welts that appear within minutes to a couple of hours of drinking. Our page on [itchy skin after drinking](/never-hungover/itchy-skin-after-drinking) covers these in more depth. These can come from histamine, sulfites, or a true allergy to an ingredient. See our [alcohol allergy guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy).
- **Contact dermatitis.** Rash where alcohol-based products touch the skin, such as hand sanitizer or alcohol-heavy toners.

If you get a new rash after drinking and have never had eczema, it's more likely to be one of these than new-onset eczema. A doctor can tell them apart.

## Why Alcohol Can Trigger an Eczema Flare

There isn't a single mechanism. Several things happen at once, and each one nudges eczema skin in the wrong direction.

### 1. It widens blood vessels in the skin

Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes and widens small blood vessels. More blood flows near the surface, the skin gets warmer and redder, and warm, inflamed skin tends to itch more. Heat is a well-known eczema trigger, and a warm bar, a dance floor, and a few drinks can add up quickly.

### 2. It can raise histamine levels

Histamine is the chemical behind much of the itch in allergic skin. Alcohol affects it in a few ways:

- Some drinks contain histamine themselves. **Red wine** tends to have more than white wine or spirits, and some beers and aged or fermented drinks also contain notable amounts.
- Alcohol appears to interfere with **diamine oxidase (DAO)**, the main enzyme your gut uses to break down histamine from food and drink.
- Acetaldehyde, the by-product your body makes while processing alcohol, can prompt immune cells called mast cells to release histamine.

For people who are sensitive to histamine, the result can be more itching, flushing, or hives. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) covers this in more depth.

### 3. It disrupts sleep, and poor sleep feeds the itch-scratch cycle

Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep later in the night. Eczema itch is often worse at night anyway, and broken sleep lowers your tolerance for itch and makes unconscious scratching more likely. Scratching damages the skin barrier, which causes more inflammation and more itch. A single rough night won't wreck your skin, but repeated nights can keep a flare going. If this sounds familiar, see [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### 4. It may dry out the skin

Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone that helps you hold onto water. Mild dehydration isn't the same as dry skin, and drinking water alone won't fix an eczema barrier. Still, many people notice their skin feels tighter and drier the morning after a heavy night, and dry skin is the starting point for most eczema flares. Our guide on whether [alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains how much this really happens.

### 5. It can feed general inflammation

Heavy drinking is linked to higher levels of inflammatory signals throughout the body, and some studies have found that people who drink more tend to have higher levels of IgE, the antibody involved in allergic reactions. These are associations, not proof of cause, and they're more relevant to heavy, regular drinking than to an occasional night out. For a broader look, see our guide to [alcohol and inflammation](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-inflammation-complete-health-impact-guide-2025).

### 6. Additives and other ingredients

Wine, beer, and cider often contain **sulfites**, which can cause reactions in a minority of people, particularly those with asthma. Beer and some spirits contain grains, yeast, and hops, and cocktails can carry citrus, dyes, preservatives, and flavorings. Any of these could be a personal trigger. Sulfites are more often linked to breathing symptoms and hives than to classic eczema, but if you react strongly to wine and not to clear spirits, they're worth considering. See our guide on [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

### 7. What happens around the drinking

This is easy to overlook. Nights out often come with salty food, late nights, sweating, smoke, skipped skincare, and sometimes stress. People also tend to forget their usual moisturizer or nighttime cream after drinking. Some of what gets blamed on alcohol is really the night that came with it.

## Which Drinks Are Most Likely to Trigger Eczema?

There's no research ranking drinks for eczema specifically, and individual reactions vary. Based on what each drink contains, here's a reasonable guide to where to start if you're experimenting:

| Drink | Possible eczema-relevant factors | General note |
|---|---|---|
| Red wine | Higher histamine, sulfites, other plant compounds | The most commonly reported culprit for skin and flushing reactions |
| White and sparkling wine | Sulfites, some histamine | Often tolerated better than red, but not always |
| Beer and cider | Histamine, yeast, grains, hops, sulfites in some ciders | A frequent trigger for people sensitive to histamine |
| Dark spirits (whiskey, brandy, dark rum) | Congeners (by-products of fermentation and aging) | More flavor compounds than clear spirits |
| Clear spirits (vodka, gin) with a plain mixer | Fewest additives | Often the best tolerated, though the alcohol itself still dilates blood vessels |
| Sugary cocktails | Dyes, citrus, preservatives, lots of sugar | Hard to pin down which ingredient is the problem |

The pattern many people find is that a measured amount of a clear spirit with soda water bothers their skin less than the same amount of alcohol from red wine or beer. That's a reasonable experiment to run, not a guarantee.

### Wine and eczema

Red wine is the drink most often blamed, and it does contain more histamine and other active plant compounds than most drinks. If wine is your problem, try white or a lower-sulfite wine, keep to one glass, and see whether the reaction changes. "Sulfite-free" labels are less common than people think, because yeast makes some sulfites naturally during fermentation.

### Beer and eczema

Beer is brewed from grains and yeast and can contain histamine. Some people with eczema notice that beer bothers their skin more than spirits. If you suspect gluten (you have diagnosed celiac disease or a confirmed wheat allergy), talk to your doctor, because those conditions have their own skin effects and need proper testing rather than guessing.

## Alcohol and Eczema on the Face

Facial eczema often gets worse with alcohol because the face flushes more than other areas. The cheeks, eyelids, and around the mouth are thin-skinned and sensitive, so the warmth and redness from drinking can show up there first. A few things help:

- Apply your usual moisturizer or barrier cream before you go out and again before bed.
- Keep makeup removal gentle. Use a non-foaming cleanser rather than scrubbing.
- If you use a prescribed cream such as **tacrolimus or pimecrolimus**, know that some people get facial flushing or a warm, red feeling when they drink alcohol while using these creams. It's a known and usually harmless side effect, but it can look like a flare. Mention it to your dermatologist if it bothers you.
- Don't confuse rosacea with eczema. Rosacea also flares with alcohol, but it causes persistent central facial redness and sometimes acne-like bumps. If you're not sure which one you have, a dermatologist can tell you, since treatment differs. Our page on whether [alcohol causes acne](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-acne) covers some of the overlap.

## Alcohol-Based Hand Sanitizer and Skincare

This is a different question from drinking, but it comes up often. Alcohol in products you put on your skin can sting broken eczema patches and strip oils from the surface.

- **Hand sanitizer** with 60% alcohol or more is effective against germs but drying. If you have hand eczema, washing with a gentle soap-free cleanser and moisturizing right after is often kinder. When you do need sanitizer, choose one with added moisturizers and apply hand cream afterward.
- **Toners, astringents, and some fragranced products** use drying alcohols such as ethanol or "alcohol denat." These are often best avoided on eczema-prone skin.
- **Fatty alcohols** such as cetyl, stearyl, and cetearyl alcohol are a different thing entirely. They are waxy moisturizing ingredients and usually fine for eczema skin. Seeing "alcohol" on a label doesn't automatically mean a product is drying.

## Eczema Medications and Alcohol

If you use only moisturizers and topical steroid creams, there's no direct interaction with drinking. The picture changes with some prescription treatments. Always check with your doctor or pharmacist about your specific medicine.

- **Methotrexate.** Used for severe eczema in some cases. Both methotrexate and alcohol can harm the liver, so doctors usually advise keeping alcohol very low or avoiding it. See our guide to [methotrexate and alcohol](/never-hungover/methotrexate-and-alcohol).
- **Cyclosporine.** Can affect the kidneys and raise blood pressure, and it is processed by the liver. Ask your prescriber about alcohol limits.
- **Oral steroids (such as prednisone).** Short courses are common for bad flares. Combining them with alcohol can increase the risk of stomach irritation.
- **Sedating antihistamines** such as hydroxyzine or diphenhydramine (Benadryl) are sometimes used at night for itch. Alcohol adds to their drowsiness, which can be risky, so don't combine them on a night you drink. Our guide to [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) explains the difference between drowsy and non-drowsy types.
- **Biologic injections (such as dupilumab) and JAK inhibitor pills.** There's no well-known direct interaction with moderate drinking, but some of these medicines require regular blood tests, including liver tests. Ask your prescriber what's sensible for you.
- **Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus).** As noted above, these can cause alcohol-related facial flushing in some people.

## How to Drink With Eczema: Practical Steps

If you want to keep drinking socially and limit the effect on your skin, these steps are sensible and low-risk.

### Before you drink

- **Moisturize well.** A good barrier layer helps skin cope with heat, sweat, and dryness.
- **Eat a real meal.** Drinking on a full stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which can soften flushing.
- **Pick your drink on purpose.** If you're still figuring out your triggers, start with a clear spirit and a plain mixer rather than red wine or beer.
- **Dress for heat.** Breathable cotton layers are better than wool or tight synthetic fabrics if you'll be somewhere warm.

### While you drink

- **Set a limit and space your drinks.** Fewer drinks over more time means less vasodilation at any moment.
- **Alternate with water.** It won't prevent a flare by itself, but it helps with dehydration and naturally slows your pace.
- **Notice early signs.** If your skin starts to feel hot and itchy, that's a good point to switch to water.

### After you drink

- **Do your normal skincare before bed,** even if you're tired. A lukewarm rinse and a generous layer of moisturizer can make a real difference by morning.
- **Keep the bedroom cool.** Heat at night worsens itch.
- **Don't take a sedating antihistamine after drinking.** If you need help with itch on drinking nights, ask a pharmacist about non-drowsy options and timing.
- **Cover hot spots** or keep nails short if you tend to scratch in your sleep.

### Keep a simple trigger diary

For two to four weeks, note what you drank, how much, what you ate, how you slept, and how your skin looked the next day and the day after. Flares can lag by a day or more, which makes them hard to link by memory. A diary often shows whether it's alcohol in general, one type of drink, or something else entirely, like stress or a change in weather.

### Try a short break

If you're not sure whether alcohol matters for you, take a few weeks off and watch your skin. If it clearly improves, you have your answer. If nothing changes, alcohol probably isn't a big factor for you, and you can focus on other triggers.

## When Eczema Symptoms After Drinking Need a Doctor

Most post-drinking skin flare-ups are uncomfortable rather than dangerous. These are the signs that mean you should get checked:

**Book an appointment with your doctor or dermatologist if:**

- Your eczema is getting worse or spreading despite your usual treatment.
- You're losing sleep to itch most nights.
- You get hives, lip swelling, or a stuffy nose after specific drinks and want to know whether it's an allergy.
- You're on a prescription eczema medicine and aren't sure how alcohol fits in.
- You're drinking more than you'd like to manage stress or itch-related insomnia. Your doctor can help with both the skin and the sleep.

**Get same-day care if:**

- Eczema patches become painful, hot, swollen, or start weeping yellow fluid or crusting, which can signal a bacterial infection.
- You see clusters of small blisters or punched-out sores on eczema skin, especially with a fever or feeling unwell. This can be **eczema herpeticum**, which needs prompt antiviral treatment.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if:**

- Your lips, tongue, face, or throat swell, you have trouble breathing or swallowing, or you feel faint after a drink. These are signs of a severe allergic reaction.

## Can Supplements Help?

Be wary of any product that promises to fix eczema. The basics with the best evidence are a consistent moisturizer routine, the treatments your doctor prescribes, and avoiding your known triggers.

On the drinking side, some people take a supplement before or during a night out to support how their body handles alcohol. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents eczema flares or reduces skin reactions to alcohol, and it won't change histamine or sulfite content in your drink. What it may do is support recovery the next day for some people, which is a separate question. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription eczema medicine, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

For the bigger picture on drinking in a way that's easier on your body, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover), and for alcohol's wider effects on skin, our [alcohol and skin health guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-skin-health-anti-aging-impact-analysis-2025).

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol doesn't cause eczema, but it's a common trigger for flares in people who already have it.
- The main reasons are widened blood vessels and warmer skin, histamine, disrupted sleep, drier skin, and additives like sulfites.
- Red wine and beer are the most commonly reported culprits. Clear spirits with a plain mixer are often tolerated better, but everyone is different.
- Moisturize before and after drinking, space your drinks, keep cool, and don't mix alcohol with sedating antihistamines.
- If you take methotrexate, cyclosporine, or another prescription eczema medicine, ask your doctor about alcohol.
- Infected-looking patches, clusters of blisters with fever, or any swelling or breathing trouble after a drink need prompt medical care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol make eczema worse?**

For many people, yes. Alcohol widens blood vessels in the skin, can raise histamine, disrupts sleep, and may dry the skin, all of which can make eczema itchier and redder. It doesn't affect everyone the same way, though, and some people with eczema notice no difference with moderate drinking. A short trigger diary is the best way to find out whether it matters for you.

**Can drinking alcohol cause eczema?**

There's no good evidence that drinking causes eczema in someone who has never had it. Eczema is mainly driven by genetics, the skin barrier, and the immune system. Alcohol can, however, cause flushing, hives, or a rash that can be mistaken for eczema. If you develop a new rash after drinking, a doctor can work out what it is.

**What alcohol is best for eczema?**

There's no research ranking drinks for eczema. Many people find that clear spirits such as vodka or gin with a plain mixer like soda water bother their skin less than red wine or beer, which contain more histamine and other compounds. Keeping the total amount low matters more than the type.

**Why does my skin itch after drinking alcohol?**

Itching after drinking is usually caused by alcohol widening blood vessels and warming the skin, by histamine in the drink or released by your body, or by additives such as sulfites. If the itch comes with raised welts, lip swelling, or wheezing, it may be an allergic or intolerance reaction and is worth discussing with a doctor.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking eczema medication?**

It depends on the medicine. Moisturizers and topical steroid creams don't interact with alcohol. Methotrexate and cyclosporine call for real caution because of liver and kidney effects, sedating antihistamines add to alcohol's drowsiness, and creams like tacrolimus can cause facial flushing when you drink. Ask your doctor or pharmacist about your specific treatment.

**How long after drinking does an eczema flare happen?**

Flushing and itch can start within minutes to hours, but a full flare often shows up the next day or two, partly because of poor sleep and scratching overnight. That delay makes it hard to link a flare to drinking from memory, which is why tracking it for a few weeks helps.

**Is alcohol-based hand sanitizer bad for eczema?**

It can be drying and can sting broken skin, so many people with hand eczema do better washing with a gentle, soap-free cleanser and moisturizing afterward. When you need sanitizer, choose one with added moisturizers and follow it with hand cream. Fatty alcohols in creams, such as cetearyl alcohol, are moisturizing and usually fine.

**Does DHM help with eczema after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents eczema flares or skin reactions to alcohol. Its research focuses on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal studies with limited human data. Managing your skin barrier, choosing drinks carefully, and following your prescribed treatment matter far more for eczema.
